BENECON312.topics: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

options.label: Applied mathematics, algorithms & statistical modelling
options.concept: This programme combines calculus, linear algebra, numerical methods and probability with algorithms, optimisation and statistical modelling. Students apply those methods to images, robot motion and economic data, and use probability to model decisions under uncertainty.

options.label: Mathematical modelling, Earth systems & scientific data
options.concept: This programme uses calculus, numerical methods and probability to study Earth systems. Students combine field and laboratory work with spatial data and satellite imagery to investigate climate, soils, groundwater and resource use. The renewable energy course applies technical and economic analysis to energy choices.

analysis: Both options build with mathematical methods, logic, linear algebra, computational and numerical methods, linear systems, probability and advanced calculus. Closest adds algorithm design, advanced algorithms, AI optimisation, decision-making and reinforcement learning, with research design, behavioural statistics, economics and econometrics applying probability and estimation. Networks is a supporting computational-systems course. Earth systems couples modelling with proxies, Earth observation and geospatial methods, soil and aquifer studies, geochemical modelling, climate and renewable-system assessment. Computer vision is shared and supplies transferable imagery methods; Earth Observation adds environmental GIS and remote-sensing acquisition and preprocessing. Robotics remains substantive for the closest plan. The eleven unique courses on each side give the second plan a different scientific object and different research methods. A separate pure mathematics option could use the existing logic, linear algebra, calculus and algorithmic number-theory topics, but the active subject range does not supply a coherent cumulative abstract algebra, real analysis, topology, measure theory and proof-seminar pathway. Neither option assumes a formal mathematics research requirement at UCR. Advanced Calculus supports multivariable and complex functions and differential equations within its description. Reinforcement Learning, Econometrics, Earth System Science Tools, Renewable System Design and Earth’s Resources have distinct contributions based on their respective official descriptions.

alignment.rationale: Both provide programming used to implement mathematical work; UCR is a general programming foundation.
Both use sets, logical reasoning and induction. Leiden uses proof to construct number systems and study convergence.
Both establish calculus for mathematical problem solving; UCR also introduces matrices, complex numbers and differential equations.
Both introduce estimation, confidence intervals and hypothesis tests. Leiden derives inference from probability models, while UCR connects it to research design and measurement.
Both study discrete optimisation and linear programming. Leiden emphasises combinatorial algorithms and proofs of correctness. UCR also covers heuristic search and constraints in AI.
Both directly study matrices, vector spaces and linear transformations.
Both develop numerical equation-solving, approximation and error/stability reasoning.
Both analyse linear systems using transforms. UCR concentrates on signals, filtering and feedback, while Leiden develops the theory of ordinary differential equations.
Both establish probability; UCR integrates probability distributions, inference and simulation.
Both extend calculus to functions of several variables. UCR also treats complex-valued functions and differential equations, while Leiden develops multivariable analysis in greater theoretical depth.
Both use Monte Carlo simulation to examine statistical methods. UCR uses it to study sampling distributions and applies estimators to economic data.
UCR has no separate breadth course introducing multiple areas of university mathematics through discipline-specific proof and problem work.
Logic and linear algebra do not reproduce a first abstract-algebra course.
UCR logic and optimisation courses do not reproduce the target’s dedicated combinatorics-and-optimisation component.
Year one allows nonoverlapping courses from Leiden bachelor’s programmes.
Leiden teaches mathematical writing and presentations in a dedicated seminar. UCR develops academic communication in Personal & Professional Development and course projects.
The one scheduled UCR linear-algebra course is already aligned with Linear Algebra 1; the second external course remains visible.
UCR has no topology course.
UCR Advanced Calculus includes complex functions but does not reproduce a dedicated complex-analysis course.
UCR has no measure-theory course.
UCR has no second abstract-algebra course.
UCR has no algebraic-geometry or algebraic-curves course.
Leiden’s seminar takes a practical problem from mathematical formulation through solution and communication. Neither UCR plan includes a dedicated seminar with that remit.
Leiden requires a supervised mathematics project with a thesis and seminar presentations. UCR offers independent research as a separate option.
Year three can include a designated minor, additional mathematics courses or another approved selection.
Leiden’s team project uses differential equations to answer a practical question and report findings. UCR covers some of the mathematical methods.
